children.label: Overview
children: Three phases: induction, maintenance, recovery
IV induction is used in most cases
Airway options: face mask, laryngeal mask, tracheal tube

children.label: Inhalational induction
children: Indications: young children, upper airway obstruction (epiglottitis)
Indications: lower airway foreign body, bronchopleural fistula or empyema, no accessible veins
IV agents cause apnea; inhalational agents preserve breathing
Start with 70% N2O in O2, deepen with volatile agent (halothane 1-3%)
Difficulties: slow induction, bronchospasm, laryngospasm, hiccups, pollution

children.label: Maintenance
children: Inhalational agents: sevoflurane, isoflurane, halothane 1-2 MAC with 70% N2O
IV agents and IV opioids (fentanyl, alfentanil, remifentanil)
TIVA: propofol plus opioid
Choice depends on surgery, premedication analgesia and patient response
Spontaneous ventilation suits superficial, minor procedures

children.label: Complications during maintenance
children: Airway obstruction: positioning and equipment
Laryngeal spasm: stop stimulation, deepen anesthesia, 100% O2, suxamethonium if severe
Bronchospasm: deepen anesthesia, IV or endotracheal lidocaine 1-2 mg/kg, bronchodilators
Malignant hyperthermia: volatile agents and suxamethonium trigger
Raised ICP worsened by CO2 retention
Atmospheric pollution: scavenging apparatus

children.label: Face mask
children: Correct fit for a gas-tight seal (sizes 00-6)
Hold the mandible forward, hold rather than press
Obstruction signs: soft-tissue indrawing, noisy breathing, inspiratory stridor
Guedel oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway helps
Reach proper depth before inserting an airway to avoid coughing or laryngospasm

children.label: Laryngeal mask airway
children: Insertion: head extended, mouth open, pre-deflated mask swept into laryngopharynx, inflate cuff, confirm, secure
Indications: clear airway without mask, spontaneous ventilation, difficult intubation
Contraindications: full stomach, regurgitation risk, impeded surgical access
Also thoracic surgery, prone position, pregnancy over 12 weeks

children.label: Tracheal intubation
children: Prepare equipment, experienced assistant, laryngoscope, tube patency
Indications: clear airway, airway hard to control (prone, sitting, lateral), head and neck surgery
Indications: protect from aspiration, suction, chest/abdomen/cranium surgery, respiratory failure, positive-pressure ventilation
Under GA with or without relaxant, or awake with topical spray and superior laryngeal nerve block
Relaxant: suxamethonium 1-1.5 mg/kg
Inhalational technique: halothane up to 4%, diaphragmatic breathing confirms depth

children.label: Tube details
children: Paediatric size = age/4 + 4
Adult: female 7-7.5, male 7.5-8.5
Cuff: fixation, prevents aspiration, prevents gas leak
Confirm: laryngoscope view, chest movement, vapour in tube, auscultation, capnography, X-ray
Esophageal intubation: fixed chest and distended abdomen

children.label: Complications of intubation
children: Early: lip and teeth trauma, jaw dislocation, vocal cord damage, epistaxis
Early: obstruction or kinking, bronchial intubation, arrhythmias and hypertension
Late: tracheal stenosis, mucosal damage, vocal cord ulceration, hoarseness

children.label: Recovery and extubation
children: Stop inhalational agent; reverse atracurium with neostigmine plus atropine
Extubate when reflexes return and vital signs are normal
Lateral position if risk of regurgitation
100% O2 before extubation to avoid diffusion hypoxia
Preoxygenate, then suction the tube, extubate during inspiration
Complications: laryngospasm, regurgitation, hypertension and tachycardia, glottic edema
Recovery room: BP, RR, HR, temperature, SpO2, pain compared with preoperative vitals
